### Recover the Net Wrench Before Interpreting It

Take the club as the system boundary and use one inertial frame. Let $C$ be its
center of mass, $P$ a grip reference point, and $\mathbf g$ gravitational
acceleration. For a rigid club with known mass $m$ and inertia $I_C$, the net
hand-on-club wrench satisfies

$$
\mathbf F_h=m\mathbf a_C-m\mathbf g-\mathbf F_a,
$$ {#eq-force_balance}

$$
\mathbf M_{h,C}=I_C\boldsymbol\alpha+
\boldsymbol\omega\times(I_C\boldsymbol\omega)-\mathbf M_{a,C}.
$$

The subscript $a$ collects declared non-hand external loads such as aerodynamics;
gravity has zero moment about $C$ in a uniform field. Include collision or turf
loads when present. Inertia, angular velocity, acceleration and moments must be
expressed consistently. For a flexible club, use the sum of segment momentum
balances or the distributed model; one rigid-body inertia is an approximation.

Translate the **same** hand wrench using

$$
\mathbf M_{h,P}=\mathbf M_{h,C}
+(\mathbf r_C-\mathbf r_P)\times\mathbf F_h.
$$ {#eq-moment_balance}

For any two reporting points, the general rule is

$$
\mathbf M_{h,Q}=\mathbf M_{h,P}
+(\mathbf r_P-\mathbf r_Q)\times\mathbf F_h.
$$ {#eq-couple_transform}

The sign follows directly from moments of the original forces. A pure couple
is independent of reference point; the moment component of a general wrench
with nonzero force is not. These are standard wrench transformations
[@lynch2017modern, chap. 3].

For example, a force $(0,4,0)$ N applied at $(0.5,0,0)$ m produces a moment
$(0,0,2)$ N m about the origin and zero moment about its application point.
The physical load did not change. It is inappropriate to label the two reported
moments different twisting actions by the hands.

### What Remains Unidentified

For two contact points with forces $\mathbf F_1,\mathbf F_2$ and local couples
$\mathbf C_1,\mathbf C_2$, the net wrench gives six balance equations:

$$
\mathbf F_h=\mathbf F_1+\mathbf F_2,\qquad
\mathbf M_{h,P}=\sum_{i=1}^2
\left[(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_P)\times\mathbf F_i+\mathbf C_i\right].
$$

There are generally more unknowns than observations. Even with zero local
couples, an equal-and-opposite force pair along the line joining the two contact
points leaves both net force and moment unchanged. Thus a known resultant does
not identify bilateral grip squeeze, finger pressures or joint tissue loading.
An instrumented grip or independently validated contact model adds information;
a pseudoinverse only selects a solution according to a mathematical metric.

The relation $\tau=J^\mathsf{T}w$ maps a specified external wrench to its
generalized load by virtual power. It does not turn an arbitrary net actuator
torque into the uniquely measured wrench at one hand. A pseudoinverse requires
a consistency check, its null space, a force/moment scaling convention, and a
physical allocation model.

### Power Is Invariant Under a Consistent Reference Change

For two material points on the same rigid body,
$\mathbf v_Q=\mathbf v_P+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\mathbf r_Q-\mathbf r_P)$.
Consequently,

$$
\mathbf F_h\cdot\mathbf v_P+\mathbf M_{h,P}\cdot\boldsymbol\omega
=\mathbf F_h\cdot\mathbf v_Q+\mathbf M_{h,Q}\cdot\boldsymbol\omega.
$$

The force and moment power components can change separately while their sum
does not. A comparison of "force-driven" and "couple-driven" power must declare
the reporting point. For a flexible grip/shaft, use velocities at the actual
ports and include deformation power; rigid transport is not exact.

### Account for Missing Loads Without Double Counting

If aerodynamic force and moment are omitted while measured motion is held
fixed, the inferred hand wrench is biased by

$$
\Delta\mathbf F_h=\mathbf F_a,\qquad
\Delta\mathbf M_{h,P}=\mathbf M_{a,C}
+(\mathbf r_C-\mathbf r_P)\times\mathbf F_a=\mathbf M_{a,P}.
$$

The omitted force's change in moment arm is already included in this wrench
translation. Do not add it again to a drag moment already reported about $P$.
For the illustrative force $(0,-8,0)$ N at $(0.6,0,0)$ m relative to the grip,
with zero intrinsic aerodynamic couple, the omitted moment is $(0,0,-4.8)$ N m.
These are chosen numbers, not measurements of a particular club or golfer.

Drag opposes velocity relative to the air; lift and aerodynamic couples need
separate directions. The coefficient, projected area, orientation, relative
wind and center of pressure must be supplied to make a quantitative estimate.
The fractional error in a small inferred grip moment can be large even when
the aerodynamic force is small relative to another load. That is a sensitivity
statement, not a general percentage correction to every swing.
